messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: New vari's for mdivide_left
parts:
Flight was delayed so I took the time to finish the mixed type cases for mdivide_left{_tri} which I've now pushed.

I've also updated mdivide_right to call mdivide_left with some transposes to take advantage of these.  Solving linear systems in Stan should be much faster now! :)

There's some work to be done to make optimal use of this in the distribution implementations, but this should already make a notable difference to calls to multi_normal with large numbers of dimensions.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] New vari's for mdivide_left
parts:
To make best use of this new stuff with a GP, we need to do a vari for the log determinant and rewrite multi_normal to not do a Cholesky decomposition.  Both of these should be relatively simple, as log_det has a simple form and the original multi_normal was written that way.

Cheers
Marcus

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] New vari's for mdivide_left

Then there'd be a function something like:

void llt_decomposition(const matrix_v &a, matrix_v &inv_a, var &det_a, var &logdet_a)

But it's likely more trouble than it's worth for now.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] New vari's for mdivide_left
parts:
On Sunday, February 3, 2013 1:32:49 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
I had been thinking about doing this by adding a new
pos definite matrix class type and having lazy methods
to access the decompositions.

There are very few instances in statistics of asymmetric positive definite matrices. So, if you also require symmetry, that is basically just saying that we need a covariance matrix class. I suppose you could make positive definite the parent class of covariance matrix, but that would basically be the same as having a virtual class that various kinds of covariance matrices inherit from.

I think the big use case now is that we don't have
vectorized multivariate probability functions.  That
means we potentially factor the covariance matrix multiple
times when we don't need to.

That is certainly bad, but it goes with the fact that for parameterized covariance matrices, we create first create the Cholesky factor, then multiply it by its transpose, then Cholesky decompose that. So, for a short-term goal, I think having a Cholesky factor type, plus some Jacobian helper functions, are more pressing than a covariance matrix class with caching.

Ben

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Tree of covariance matrix classes
parts: On Sunday, February 3, 2013 3:18:12 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:I was thinking covariance matrices and correlation matrices,

(and perhaps diagonal versions) but not asymmetric matrices.
Sorry if my terminology's confusing.  I'm happy to take expert
advice on naming variable types!

FWIW, here are the classes I had laid out so far:

CovarianceMatrix (abstract)
  |
  |
---- UserCovarianceMatrix (can be whatever the user implements)
  |
  |
---- DiagonalCovarianceMatrix
  |
  |
---- SaturatedCovarianceMatrix (essentially what cov_matrix is now)
  |
  |
---- CorrelationMatrix (essentially what cor_matrix is now)
  |
  |
---- ScaledCovarianceMatrix (like sigma_sq * X)
    |
    |
-------- AR1CovarianceMatrix
  |
  |
---- SandwichCovarianceMatrix (like X * A * X')
    |
    |
------- SpectralCovarianceMatrix (with X eigenvectors and A eigenvalues)
    |
    |
-------- SDsCorrelationMatrix( with X standard deviations and A a correlation matrix)
  |
  |
---- CFACovarianceMatrix (like L * P * L' + D)
    |
    |
-------- EFACovarianceMatrix (with P = I and L triangular)


Basically, anything that has a specialized calculation for either the inverse, or the determinant, or the Jacobian could have a subclass. And we would probably want to use the curiously recurring template pattern to avoid the virtual function calls.

Ben

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Tree of covariance matrix classes
parts:
On Sunday, February 3, 2013 9:44:26 PM UTC-5, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
Is it possible to avoid using the term covariance matrix in the base class?  Perhaps SymPosDefMatrix or SPDMatrix?  While most often people use covariance matrix, people also use precision matrices and things like that.  SPD is more accurate overall.

I'm not wedded to any of the names. However, the abstract class has (more than) four attributes: the covariance matrix itself, its Cholesky factor, its inverse, and the Cholesky factor of the inverse, each of which has a flag indicating whether it has been initialized since it is almost never necessary to utilize all four but almost always necessary to utilize one. And the derived classes will all have various constructors, depending on what is appropriate, so you could instantiate an object with a precision matrix and possibly the covariance matrix itself would never be calculated.

At that point, it seems like the question of whether Stan should parameterize the univariate normal in terms of the standard deviation, variance, precision, or square root of precision. And it seems to me that a covariance matrix is the canonical way of doing that for multivariate models. In other words, I don't see a precision matrix as being a separate concept, just a special name for the inverse of a covariance matrix, even though you can interpret the elements of a precision matrix in terms of one pair of variables being predicted by the others. I could see having PDMatrix being the top-level class if we were going to do anything that involved a positive definite matrix that wasn't (convertable to) a covariance matrix, although I don't see what that would be at the moment.
Also, I would prefer "FullCovarianceMatrix" versus "SaturatedCovarianceMatrix".  Saturadated just sounds like an odd term here.

Yeah, I agree Saturated is weird. UnstructuredAsideFromBeingPositiveDefiniteCovarianceMatrix would be more descriptive.

Ben
